title: Writing Community Rules People Can Follow
body:
Community rules fail when they are long, vague, or written in language only moderators understand. Members follow rules they can remember, and they remember rules that are short, concrete, and tied to the community's purpose. A rule that says to be respectful is hard to enforce fairly; a rule that names the behaviour, such as no personal attacks and no posting of private information, can be applied the same way to everyone.

Method. Write five to eight rules at most, each naming a behaviour rather than a character trait, and give one brief example per rule where the meaning could be unclear. Publish the rules where new members meet them, state what happens on a first break and on a repeated break, and review the rules with the community when the community changes. Rules that are never explained are experienced as surprises, and surprises breed resentment.

Checklist.

  • Five to eight rules at most
  • Each rule names a behaviour
  • One example where meaning could be unclear
  • Consequences stated in advance
  • Rules reviewed when the community changes

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Writing Community Rules People Can Follow. Use and limits. Do not write rules that give moderators unlimited discretion without any standard, and do not enforce an unwritten rule as if members should have known it. Where a rule touches safety or the law, such as harassment or illegal content, state that plainly and act promptly. title: Welcoming New Members
body:
A community's future is decided in a newcomer's first week, when they learn whether they are welcome, what is expected, and how to take part without embarrassment. Communities that leave newcomers to guess lose most of them silently, while communities that greet, orient, and invite a first contribution keep them. Welcoming is not a single hello message; it is a short path from arrival to first useful participation.

Method. Greet newcomers promptly and personally where the community's size allows, point them to the rules and to one good first place to take part, and pair the invitation with a low-stakes task, such as introducing themselves or answering a simple question. Watch their first contributions for a chance to respond helpfully rather than critically, and check back after a week with a second invitation if they have gone quiet.

Checklist.

  • Greet promptly and personally
  • Point to rules and one first place
  • Offer a low-stakes first task
  • Respond helpfully to first contributions
  • Check back after a week

title: Setting Expectations for Moderators
body:
Moderators burn out or overreach when their role is never defined, because they must guess how much power they hold and how much time they owe. Clear expectations name what moderators decide alone, what they decide together, how quickly they are expected to act, and when they should step back from a decision that involves them personally. A defined role protects members from arbitrary power and moderators from endless demand.

Method. Write a short moderator guide covering scope, response expectations, escalation paths, and conflicts of interest, and give new moderators a trial period with a mentor. Require moderators to explain removals briefly, to keep private member information private, and to ask a second moderator before acting on a close or contested case. Review the guide with the team regularly, since expectations that are never revisited drift.

Checklist.

  • Scope and decision rights named
  • Response expectations stated
  • Escalation path for hard cases
  • Step back from personal conflicts
  • Trial period with a mentor

Use and limits. Do not expect moderators to be available at all hours, and do not let a single moderator become the only person who can act, since that creates both burnout and a single point of failure. Moderators are volunteers or staff with limits, and a community that ignores those limits loses them. title: Handling a First Rule Break
body:
A first rule break is usually a misunderstanding rather than a challenge, and the response should teach before it punishes. A private, specific warning tells the member what happened, which rule it broke, and what to do instead, and it preserves dignity in a way a public rebuke cannot. Public punishment of a first mistake teaches the whole community to fear the moderators, which is a poor foundation for trust.

Method. Contact the member privately, quote the post or behaviour concerned, name the rule, and offer the corrected form or the alternative place for that content. Ask whether the rule was unclear, and listen to the answer, since a first break often reveals a rule that needs rewriting. Record the warning briefly and consistently, so a second break can be judged fairly against a known first.

Checklist.

  • Contact privately
  • Quote the behaviour concerned
  • Name the rule
  • Offer the corrected form
  • Record briefly and consistently

title: De-escalating a Heated Thread
body:
A heated thread is a conversation whose temperature has overtaken its topic, where participants reply to each other's tone rather than each other's points. De-escalation works by lowering the temperature without closing the topic: slow the pace, separate the people from the problem, and restate the points each side has actually made. Closing the thread at the first sign of heat teaches members that intensity ends discussion, which rewards whoever raises the temperature first.

Method. Pause the thread briefly where the pace is driving the heat, and post a calm summary that separates positions from insults, naming what each side has said fairly. Invite replies to the summary rather than to each other, enforce the rules against personal attacks evenly, and move the conversation to a slower format, such as a moderated exchange, when the open thread cannot cool. Reopen fully once the temperature has fallen.

Checklist.

  • Pause briefly where pace drives heat
  • Summarise positions fairly
  • Invite replies to the summary
  • Enforce attack rules evenly
  • Move to a slower format if needed

Use and limits. Do not take sides in the summary, and do not punish only the side whose tone offends you while excusing the other side's attacks. A summary that misrepresents one side will restart the fire it was meant to cool. title: Spam and Off-Topic Posts
body:
Spam and off-topic posts damage a community quietly, by burying the content members came for under content they did not ask for. The remedy is removal with a brief explanation, not silent deletion, because silent deletion teaches members that posts vanish for unknown reasons and makes every later removal feel arbitrary. A short note naming the rule and the right place for the content keeps removal fair and teaches at the same time.

Method. Remove the post, leave a brief note naming the rule it broke and, where one exists, the right place for that content, and apply the same standard to established members and newcomers alike. For a first off-topic post, redirect rather than punish; for repeated spam after warnings, escalate under the stated consequences. Keep a short log of removals so patterns, such as one member repeatedly testing the boundary, are visible.

Checklist.

  • Remove the post
  • Leave a brief note naming the rule
  • Name the right place where one exists
  • Apply the standard evenly
  • Log removals briefly

title: Appeals: Challenging a Moderation Decision
body:
An appeal is a community's promise that moderation can be wrong and can be corrected, and without that promise, every disputed decision becomes a permanent grievance. A fair appeal process is simple: a member can ask for review, someone other than the original moderator reviews it, the review considers the rule and the evidence, and the outcome with its reason is told to the member. Appeals do not make moderation weak; they make it trustworthy.

Method. Publish the appeal route alongside the rules, accept appeals in a private channel, and assign each appeal to a moderator who did not make the original decision. Review the post or behaviour against the written rule, not against the moderator's memory of it, and reply with the outcome and the reason, including an apology and restoration where the original decision was wrong. Record outcomes so repeated errors in the same rule become visible.

Checklist.

  • Appeal route published with the rules
  • Private appeal channel
  • Reviewer differs from original moderator
  • Review against the written rule
  • Outcome and reason told to the member

Use and limits. Do not let the original moderator review their own decision alone, and do not punish members for appealing in good faith, since punishment for appeals teaches members that the route is a trap. An appeal that is never answered is worse than no appeal route at all. title: Handling Harassment Reports
body:
A harassment report is a moment of trust: the reporter is telling moderators something painful and uncertain, and the response they receive determines whether they and others will ever report again. Good handling is private, prompt, and centred on the reporter's safety: acknowledge quickly, keep the report confidential, act on the evidence, and tell the reporter what happened in general terms without exposing private details of the process. The reporter's safety outranks the community's curiosity about the case.

Method. Acknowledge the report within a day, keep it visible only to the moderators handling it, and preserve the evidence before any content is removed. Assess the pattern, not just the single incident, since harassment is often a series, and act proportionately, from warnings to removal to banning, under the stated consequences. Tell the reporter the outcome in general terms, offer support options the community can genuinely provide, and never require the reporter to confront the reported person.

Checklist.

  • Acknowledge within a day
  • Keep the report confidential
  • Preserve evidence before removal
  • Assess the pattern, not one incident
  • Tell the reporter the outcome in general terms

Use and limits. Do not share report details with the wider community, do not ask the reporter to prove harm beyond what the evidence shows, and do not delay action while seeking a perfect account of events. Where a report involves a crime or a risk of physical harm, direct the reporter to the appropriate authority and act on the community side without waiting. title: Moderating a Live Chat or Event
body:
Live moderation differs from forum moderation because there is no time to deliberate: messages arrive in seconds, and a harmful message is visible the moment it appears. Live moderators therefore work from preparation rather than reaction, with agreed signals, a second moderator watching, and pre-written responses for the cases that recur. A live event with one unprepared moderator is an event waiting for its worst moment.

Method. Before the event, agree on the rules, the signals for help, and who removes, who warns, and who watches. During the event, keep two moderators where possible, one watching the chat and one handling removals, and use slow mode or follower-only mode when the pace overwhelms the team. After the event, review what happened, thank the team, and update the preparation for the next event from what was learned.

Checklist.

  • Rules and signals agreed in advance
  • Two moderators where possible
  • Roles split: watch and act
  • Slow mode when pace overwhelms
  • Review after the event

title: Recruiting and Training Volunteer Moderators
body:
A moderation team is built, not found: the best future moderators are usually the members already helping others, answering questions, and calming threads without being asked. Recruiting from that visible helpfulness beats open applications, which attract people who want power more than people who want to help. Training then turns helpful members into consistent moderators, by showing them real cases and the reasoning behind real decisions.

Method. Watch for members who help consistently and fairly, invite them privately, and explain the workload and the limits honestly before they accept. Train with real past cases, anonymised, asking trainees to decide and then comparing their reasoning with the actual outcome. Pair each new moderator with a mentor, start them on low-stakes tasks, and review their early decisions kindly and promptly, so training continues after the invitation.

Checklist.

  • Recruit from visible helpfulness
  • Explain workload and limits honestly
  • Train with anonymised real cases
  • Pair with a mentor
  • Start on low-stakes tasks

title: Transparency: Moderation Logs and Reports
body:
Transparency lets a community check that moderation is fair without exposing the private details of individual cases. A public log that counts actions by type, rule, and outcome, without naming members or quoting private reports, shows patterns the community can judge: whether one rule is enforced far more than others, whether appeals succeed, and whether the workload is growing. Transparency without privacy, by contrast, turns accountability into exposure.

Method. Publish regular summaries counting removals, warnings, bans, and appeal outcomes by rule and by outcome, with no member names and no private report content. Explain any large change in the numbers, such as a spam wave or a rule change, in plain words, and invite questions about the summaries themselves. Keep the detailed case records private to the handling moderators, and say so, so members understand what the summaries can and cannot show.

Checklist.

  • Summaries count actions by rule and outcome
  • No member names in public summaries
  • No private report content published
  • Large changes explained plainly
  • Detailed case records stay private

title: Conflict Between Members
body:
A conflict between two members is not the same as a rule break: both may have followed the rules while still misunderstanding, competing for, or resenting each other, and punishment will not resolve it. Mediation resolves it by giving each side a heard account, a shared statement of what happened, and an agreement about future behaviour that both can keep. The moderator's job in mediation is to hold the process fairly, not to declare a winner.

Method. Speak to each member privately first, hear each account without interruption, and check what each side actually wants, which is often recognition or a change in future behaviour rather than punishment. Bring the sides together only when both are willing, restate a shared account both accept, and agree specific future behaviours with a date to review. Follow up at that date, and reopen the process if the agreement has not held.

Checklist.

  • Hear each side privately first
  • Check what each side actually wants
  • Bring sides together only when willing
  • Agree specific future behaviours
  • Follow up at a review date

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for Conflict Between Members. title: Protecting Younger and Vulnerable Members
body:
Communities that include younger or vulnerable members carry a higher duty of care, because those members may not recognise manipulation, may share personal information freely, and may struggle to report harm. Protection starts with design: private contact between adults and minors is restricted, personal information is never requested or shared, and reporting is easy, private, and believed. A community that treats all members as equally robust will fail the members who need its care most.

Method. Restrict private messaging where younger members are present, prohibit requests for personal information, age, location, or images, and make reporting a single visible action with a private channel behind it. Train moderators to recognise grooming patterns and to escalate immediately rather than investigating alone, and involve a responsible adult or appropriate authority where a young person's safety is at risk. Review the protections regularly with safeguarding guidance for the community's setting.

Checklist.

  • Restrict private adult-minor contact
  • Prohibit personal information requests
  • Reporting is one visible action
  • Escalate grooming concerns immediately
  • Involve responsible adults where safety is at risk

title: Closing a Thread Without Shutting Down Discussion
body:
Closing a thread is sometimes necessary, when it has run its course, drifted beyond recovery, or become a place where the same points repeat without progress. A good closure honours what the thread achieved: it summarises the discussion, names the outcome or the reason for closing, and points members to where the conversation can continue. A closure that merely locks the door without explanation feels like censorship, even when it was genuinely housekeeping.

Method. Before closing, summarise the thread fairly, including views you disagree with, and state the reason for closing in one plain sentence. Point to the place where the topic continues, such as a new thread, a decision record, or a related channel, and invite members to continue there rather than reopening the closed thread. Leave the thread readable where possible, so the discussion remains part of the community's memory rather than a vanished argument.

Checklist.

  • Summarise fairly before closing
  • State the reason in one plain sentence
  • Point to where discussion continues
  • Invite continuation in the new place
  • Leave the thread readable where possible

Use and limits. Do not close a thread to end an argument you are losing, and do not close threads silently during a controversy, since silent closure during controversy will be read as suppression whatever the true reason. Closure must be explainable to a member who disagrees with it. title: Moderator Burnout and Rotation
body:
Moderation work is emotionally heavy: moderators read the worst content, absorb members' anger, and make contested decisions, often as volunteers in their spare time. Without rotation, rest, and support, good moderators burn out, become harsher or more distant, and eventually leave, taking their experience with them. Sustainable moderation treats rest as part of the work, not as a reward for surviving it.

Method. Rotate demanding duties, such as report handling and live moderation, so no one carries them continuously, and give moderators real time off with cover arranged in advance. Provide a private moderator space for debriefing difficult cases, recognise the work publicly without exposing private case details, and check in regularly with moderators who have handled hard cases. Make stepping back easy and respected, so a moderator can rest before burning out rather than after.

Checklist.

  • Rotate demanding duties
  • Real time off with cover arranged
  • Private space for debriefing
  • Public recognition without case exposure
  • Stepping back easy and respected

Use and limits. Do not treat burnout as a personal failure, and do not keep a burned-out moderator on the hardest duties because no replacement is ready; that choice harms both the moderator and the members they serve. title: Reviewing Rules Over Time
body:
Rules written for a small community rarely fit the same community grown large, and rules written for one era rarely fit the next. Regular review keeps rules alive: members are invited to say which rules help, which confuse, and which are enforced unevenly, and the community revises together rather than discovering drift through disputes. A rule set that is never reviewed becomes either a museum or a weapon, depending on who invokes it.

Method. Review the rules at fixed intervals, such as twice a year, and after any major incident or growth spurt, inviting member feedback in a structured form rather than an open argument. Publish what changed and why, give members time to learn changes before enforcing them, and archive old versions so members can see how the rules evolved. Treat enforcement data from the transparency log as evidence in the review, since patterns there show which rules need rewriting.

Checklist.

  • Review at fixed intervals
  • Invite structured member feedback
  • Publish what changed and why
  • Time to learn before enforcement
  • Archive old versions
